title: A brutal realization
author: Red__Ace
selftext:
I recently launched my first android game: History Quiz: Chrono Clash [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.chronoclash.app&hl=en-US](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.chronoclash.app&hl=en-US)   


It took me about 2-3 months of almost endless cycles of fixing, testing, adding new features, retesting, fixing, retesting.... During this, there were many 16 hour continuous sessions working on this. Planning, fixing, and changing how matchmaking claims, firestore reads/ writes, rewards, ranks, leaderboards, achievements, and the different game modes all work was hard even with Codex and Claude. 

Even harder was optimizing the firebase usage while still keeping all functionality intact and secure, begging tester friends every few days to play the new update so I can test all features, generating images for almost 500 assets, and reiterating them until I could a relatively decent image.   
  
Finally, completed the play store review, optimized store listing, icons, screenshots, feature graphics, videos, worked on ASO, and launched the app. Aaaaaaaand nothing. No visibility.  
  
Then it hit me. The bitter truth about production - it's not the hard part producing it and definitely not the part that matters the most. A below average game/ app with strong marketing will always outperform an excellent app with little marketing.   
  
I was enjoying building it, I learnt so much about coding and apps, the different frameworks, the backend and so much more through this project, but I was being way too detailed, obsessed with optimization for a game I did not even know would get any attention or traffic. 

It is disappointing, but I have not stopped. I'm still working on other games that are not as niche. I have finally been allowed to express my ideas that were limited due to not knowing how to program or code, and I will continue working on them!

I'm working on 3 other games right now, close to launching them soon too, while trying to share my experience with my first ever app; Chrono Clash and trying to put it out there.   
My other games in Production: [RedAce Studios](https://redacestudios.pages.dev/)

comments.author: random_account6721

replies.author: Red__Ace
replies.body:

With AI coding tools, the time it takes for experienced teams will also drop down fairly quickly, so the old timings become outdated. It is only now that the AI has gotten good enough, even though it has been around for some time now.

comments.author: Latter-Confusion-654
comments.body:
5 days post-launch is too early to call. Google takes 5-7 days just to fully index your metadata, and that's before the algorithm has any traction signals to rank you. Right now your data mostly says "I haven't been discoverable yet", not "marketing is the issue".

The marketing-vs-quality framing oversimplifies it imo. ASO is marketing and costs nothing. For a history trivia game specifically, you can rank on "history quiz", "history trivia" etc., less saturated than general trivia.

Push 5-10 reviews from friends/family, wait 2-3 weeks, then check which keywords you actually rank on (applyra.io free tier shows this). If you're still flat with metadata working, then yes, channels become the focus.

comments.author: imnotabot303
comments.body:
That's just the reality of indi game dev. 2-3 months is actually nothing in terms of normal game dev time, people regularly spend a few years making a game only for it to fail. 

Making successful games is hard and AI isn't going to make it any easier, all that's really going to be happening is that you're competing with more people churning out AI games. The easier it becomes for people to make games with AI the less chance you have of anyone being interested in your AI game.

These type of games are creeping into spaces like the play store more and more, most of them, just like yours, has obvious AI art and an AI logo. Most people wil simply ignore it on that alone.

It's good you had fun making it but what you experienced is the norm and it will only get worse the easier it is for games like this to be made.

comments.author: Asphyxa
comments.body:
I’m just creating a game idea I always wanted to play myself but didn’t really find anything on the market scratching my itch fully. It’s a very autism style kind of game with heavy management but I always find the games in this category to be a bit limiting and too arcady so I’m making my own. I actually do it to be able to play it myself someday. I have a full time job in finance and this is my side project so I don’t really care if it gains attention or not. I do all the art myself, will probably buy map sprites though as I don’t enjoy doing that. I only enjoy drawing warriors. 

So my main advice would be to do it for yourself and think less about what other people want. But yeah if you’re trying to vibecode as a line of profession my advice obviously shouldn’t be taken. But I personally think trying to make an easy buck from vibecoding apps is not the way to go really and a lot of people pressure themselves into this without having a solid game idea and release the game way too soon without it being fully developed or even checking if theres a market demand. If you do it as a fun project for yourself you don’t need to care about market demand. I do my game because theres nothing on the market and I want to play it myself. I might not even release it since I don’t want the pressure from customers to add stuff I might promise when I feel optimistic.

comments.author: Ludagon
comments.body:
First up, congrats on releasing! 

I haven't published on Android for years so I can't remember the dev pages for Google Play, but do you get any stats on how many people have actually viewed your app page (but not downloaded)? If you get to see that kind of info, it can help in figuring out whether nobody is noticing your game, or heaps of people are looking into it but there's something in the store description and screens that's not appealing to your potential players.

Hope it picks up for you, but if not it sounds like you still learnt a lot about various components that you might be able to use in future games.
